entities.summary:
Shaddad, a legendary Arabian tyrant, was the ruler of the lost city of Iram of the Pillars, a place described in the Qur'an as a major center of Arabian culture. According to Arabian folklore, Shaddad was the son of 'Ad al-Miltat ibn Saksak ibn Wa'il ibn Himyar, and his reign was marked by tyranny and oppression. Shaddad's reign is often seen as a symbol of the decline of the Arabian Peninsula's pre-Islamic era.

Shaddad's legacy is complex and multifaceted, reflecting the tumultuous history of the Arabian Peninsula. His story has been retold and reinterpreted in various forms of art and literature, including poetry and music. The Iram of the Pillars, a city believed to be Shaddad's capital, is said to have been destroyed by a devastating flood, which was sent by Allah as a punishment for Shaddad's tyranny.

The impact of Shaddad's reign can be seen in the many regional and cultural movements that followed in the Arabian Peninsula. His legacy has also influenced Islamic art and architecture, with many mosques and palaces built in the style of the Iram of the Pillars. Despite the passage of centuries, Shaddad remains an important figure in Arabian folklore, symbolizing the complexities and contradictions of the region's history.

Shaddad's story serves as a reminder of the enduring power of myth and legend in shaping our understanding of the past. His legacy continues to captivate audiences around the world, inspiring new works of art and literature that explore the complexities of Arabian culture and history.

The archaeological site of Iram of the Pillars, believed to be Shaddad's capital, has been the subject of much speculation and debate. While its exact location remains unknown, many historians believe that it was located in modern-day Yemen, based on descriptions of the city in ancient texts.
